title: All About Alligators
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss alligators: their size and lifespan, small brains but surprising problem-solving, freshwater habitat and alligator dens as a keystone species, armor plating (osteoderms), speed and stamina, nictitating membranes and the palatal valve for underwater life, lurking and feeding behavior including the death roll, bite strength compared with crocodiles, rarity of attacks on humans, near-extinction from the hide trade and recovery after protection, temperature-dependent sex determination and maternal nest protection, expansion into Tennessee and overwintering under ice, how to tell alligators from crocodiles, Florida's regulated hunting program, and a listener mail segment. Includes a few off-topic tangents (Matrix films, Steve Winwood, a sponsor break).

segments.title: Opening banter and alligator sightings
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about watching alligators walk, a Hitchcock theme tangent, and Josh's Okefenokee canoe trip where alligators surrounded camp. They compare alligators with crocodiles and cite Florida population numbers.

segments.title: Alligator brain and intelligence
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the alligator's small brain relative to its body and anecdotal evidence of smart behavior such as climbing fences, escaping enclosures, and using sticks as lures. They attribute the description to a HowStuffWorks article.

segments.title: Alligator classification, size and tails
segments.summary: Alligators are reptiles in the order Crocodilia, which has existed for over 180 million years. The hosts describe growth, tail fat storage, typical adult sizes, and the famous alligator Utan at Alligator Adventures.

segments.title: Alligator feeding and fat reserves
segments.summary: Alligators need little food and can go long periods without eating, using fat reserves. Captive feeding shows are mentioned, and the hosts note alligators swallow prey in bite-sized chunks.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A short mid-episode break with a sponsor read.

segments.title: Lifespan and freshwater habitat
segments.summary: The hosts discuss wild versus captive lifespans and then note alligators live in freshwater, using ponds, lakes, rivers, and canals. Alligator dens dug into the water table act as refuges for other animals, making them a keystone species.

segments.title: Armor plating and speed
segments.summary: The hosts describe osteoderms, the bony plates under alligator skin that make them hard to cut and hard to hunt. They note alligators can run about eleven miles per hour on land in a straight line, and that zigzagging is a bad escape strategy. Stamina is limited.

segments.title: Underwater adaptations and salt glands
segments.summary: Alligators lack salt glands, which is why they prefer fresh water. Adaptations include nictitating membranes that let them see underwater, closable ear and nostril flaps, and the palatal valve that keeps water out of the lungs and lets them hold prey underwater.

segments.title: Ambush feeding, bite strength, and the death roll
segments.summary: Alligators are lurkers who wait motionless for prey. Their teeth are built for crushing, and their bite strength is compared with crocodiles and lions and tigers. Alligators drown and roll prey, using twist feeding (the death roll), and then stash and tear apart food. Attacks on humans are rare.

segments.title: Hide trade, near extinction, and recovery
segments.summary: Early settlers killed alligators to protect livestock. Demand for alligator leather in the early twentieth century nearly drove the species to extinction. Florida banned hunting in 1962 and federal protection followed, after which the population recovered. Alligator breeding and nest protection by mothers are described, along with temperature-dependent sex determination.

segments.title: Alligators in Tennessee, cold weather, and telling species apart
segments.summary: Alligators have expanded their range into Tennessee. They survive freezing winters by keeping their snouts above ice while the water beneath stays warmer. The hosts describe how to tell alligators from crocodiles by snout shape and visible teeth, and mention a myth about birds cleaning crocodile teeth.

segments.title: Florida hunting program and safety tips
segments.summary: Florida runs a limited permit hunting program that the hosts say has kept the population stable. Legal methods include the bang stick and fishing gear, and the hosts raise concerns about unethical hunts and poaching. Safety advice includes never feeding alligators, keeping pets away from ponds, and fighting back if attacked.

segments.title: Listener mail from Louise
segments.summary: Louise writes in with a gentle ribbing about the hosts' comments on blood going through water treatment, noting menstruation. The hosts thank her.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listener mail and mention the iHeart Radio app.
